title: Risk-Aware Joint Inference and Resource Control for Physical AI in 6G Networks
comment: Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Wireless edge inference enables Physical-AI devices to execute edge-inferred actions using transmitted sensory inputs. Since the risk of incorrect actions vary across observations and tasks, the associated uplink transmission of sensory inputs requires different levels of wireless reliability. For instance, applying a fixed signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) requirement can overprovision low-risk tasks while underprovisioning high-risk ones. Therefore, we propose risk-aware control for edge inference (RACE), which maps predicted action-failure probability and task criticality to adaptive SINR targets and combines them with deadline-derived SINR requirements. A slow-timescale large language model (LLM) proposes task requirements for deterministic validation, while a fast hybrid actor selects inference configurations and transmit power levels, complemented by analytical receive beamforming and finite power restoration. Simulations show $11\%$ improvement in the average accuracy-latency-energy objective over fixed-high-SINR control, with near-zero constraint outage.

title: CuEVM: Scaling Smart Contract Execution on GPUs
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Data Engineering 2027 (ICDE 2027). DOI to be updated
summary: Smart contracts on Ethereum blockchain process transactions worth billions of US dollars daily. They run on top of Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) which executes transactions sequentially. This execution model creates a performance bottleneck, especially for new blockchain workloads with large numbers of transactions, such as security testing. We present CuEVM, a GPU-native and semantically complete EVM execution engine that treats transaction execution as a massively parallel data processing problem. It employs novel data structures and GPU-aware scheduling to accelerate execution. Unlike prior works that transpile the contract and rely on a host CPU for many operations, CuEVM supports complete EVM semantics natively on the GPU. It passes 100% of the Ethereum VMTests and 96.2% of the full execution-test suite. On a single commodity GPU, CuEVM executes over 8 million ERC-20 transfers per second, outperforming existing baselines by up to two orders of magnitude. We build a smart contract fuzzer, called CuEVM-fuzz, on top of CuEVM. The fuzzer achieves over a million end-to-end executions per second, up to 23x and 4.8x higher than the state-of-the-art CPU-based and GPU-based baselines, respectively.

title: Sparse Matrix Multiplication Exponent 1.5 in the Low-bandwidth Model
summary:
We study sparse matrix multiplication in the low-bandwidth model: $n$ computers multiply two $n\times n$ matrices, and each computer can send and receive one $O(\log n)$-bit message per round. The input matrices are uniformly sparse, meaning that there are at most $d$ nonzero entries in each row and column, and the task is to compute a uniformly sparse part of their product.
  In prior work, Gupta et al.~(SPAA 2022) presented an $O(d^{1.907})$-round algorithm over fields for this problem when the sparsity structure is globally known in advance (this is referred to as the supported setting). The upper bound was later improved to $O(d^{1.832})$ rounds.
  In this work, we give a deterministic algorithm that solves this problem in $O(d^{3/2})$ rounds in the supported setting, improving the previous bounds over fields and semirings.

title: Plurality Consensus for $h$-Majority via First-Repetition Rules
summary: In the h-Majority dynamics, each of n agents holds one of k opinions and, in every synchronous round, observes the opinions of h agents chosen independently and uniformly at random and adopts a most frequent one among them, breaking ties uniformly at random. Let M_0 be the initial number of agents holding the most frequent opinion, and Delta_0 its bias, its lead over the second most frequent opinion. We show that, for every sample size h >= 3, if Delta_0 >= L sqrt(M_0 log n) max{1, n/(h^2 M_0)} for a sufficiently large constant L, then h-Majority reaches consensus on the initially most frequent opinion within O((1 + n/(h^2 M_0)) log n) rounds with high probability. This is the time bound proved for the DejaVu dynamics with h samples (arXiv:2604.03648); our bias condition is that of DejaVu when h >= sqrt(n/M_0), and larger by a factor sqrt(n/(h^2 M_0)) otherwise. Our main contribution, the analysis of one round, rests on a comparison principle: among all rules that read the same observations and treat opinions symmetrically, plurality maximizes the difference between the probability of outputting the most frequent opinion and that of outputting any fixed competitor. We apply it to the rule that adopts the first opinion repeated among h-1 observations, and otherwise the h-th observation: its output law is the law of the new opinion of a random agent after one round of DejaVu with h-1 samples. Hence, in expectation, one round of h-Majority widens the gap between the most frequent opinion and each competitor at least as much as that round of DejaVu, whose analysis we use as a black box. Independently and concurrently, d'Amore, Rybicki, Shimizu, Shiraga and Vacus (arXiv:2610.40562) obtained, among other results, the same time bound under the weaker bias condition of DejaVu, with a different analysis of one round and a martingale analysis over many rounds.

title: Context Graph: Explainable Multi-Agent Decision Chains in AI-RAN
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: AI-RAN distributes network control across multiple autonomous agents, namely xApps and rApps operating over shared radio resources. When an alert or degradation appears, operators currently lack a structured way to trace which decision caused it, what context triggered that decision, and how other agents interacted. Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.

title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
summary: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

title: MegaOps: A Kernel Overlapping Framework with PyTorch-like Modularity and Megakernel Performance
summary: Modern ML frameworks execute models using the kernel-per-operator paradigm, which runs each operator as a separate GPU kernel. This paradigm is modular, since developers can compose various kernel implementations and profile each kernel in isolation. However, this paradigm enforces dependencies at the granularity of entire kernels, which places a barrier between dependent kernels. These barriers cause streaming multiprocessors to idle, serialize computation and communication, and prevent a kernel from prefetching its weights while the preceding kernel runs. Megakernels remove kernel barriers by fusing the operators of an entire layer or model into a single kernel, but they give up the modularity of the kernel-per-operator paradigm. In this work, we ask whether a kernel-per-operator ML framework can perform on par with megakernels. Our key insight is that removing kernel barriers does not require fusing kernels. We develop MegaOps, a framework that launches dependent kernels on separate CUDA streams and enforces each dependency on individual tiles of the intermediate tensor that the producer kernel writes and the consumer kernel reads. Since kernels synchronize on data tiles instead of on each other's thread blocks, any two kernels that adopt the same data tiling can be composed without modifying either kernel. We evaluate MegaOps on dense Llama3 and Qwen3 models on single H100, A100, and L40 GPUs and on multi-GPU servers with 4$\times$A100 and 8$\times$H100. Our MegaOps framework matches the throughput of hand-tuned ThunderKittens megakernels, and achieves 1.09$\times$-1.10$\times$ the decode throughput and 0.98$\times$-1.10$\times$ the prefill throughput of the best-performing baseline, while reusing existing Triton, cuBLAS, and cuDNN kernels.

title: Smoothed Analysis for Distributed MIS
summary:
We study smoothed analysis of the distributed Maximal Independent Set (MIS) problem. Luby's algorithm computes an MIS in $O(\log n)$ rounds, while the recent $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$ lower bound of Khoury and Schild (2026) shows that it is nearly optimal even in the LOCAL model. We ask whether small random perturbations can overcome this worst-case barrier.
  Given an arbitrary base graph $G$ on $n$ nodes, we consider the smoothed graph $\mathcal{G}_s=G\triangle G(n,p)$, where $G(n,p)$ is an independent random graph and $\triangle$ denotes symmetric difference. Thus, each possible edge is independently toggled with probability $p$.
  We establish nearly tight bounds on the smoothing needed for faster distributed MIS. For every base graph $G$, when $p=β\ln n/n$ for a sufficiently large constant $β$, a randomized LOCAL algorithm, given only $\mathcal{G}_s$, computes an MIS of $\mathcal{G}_s$ in $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ rounds with high probability. This is almost quadratically faster than the worst-case lower bound. Conversely, if $p\le(1/2-δ)\ln n/n$ for a fixed constant $δ>0$, there exists a base graph on which every randomized LOCAL MIS algorithm requires $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$ rounds on the smoothed graph. Hence, the smoothing parameter required for this speedup is optimal up to a constant factor.
  These results show that smoothed analysis can overcome worst-case lower-bound barriers for distributed local graph problems.

title: Snoopie: A Multi-GPU Communication Profiler and Visualizer
comment: Published at ICS '24" with the DOI 10.1145/3650200.3656597
summary: With data movement becoming one of the most expensive bottlenecks in computing, the need for profiling tools to analyze communication becomes crucial for effectively scaling multi-GPU applications. While existing profiling tools including first-party software by GPU vendors are robust and excel at capturing compute operations within a single GPU, support for monitoring GPU-GPU data transfers and calls issued by communication libraries is currently inadequate. To fill these gaps, we introduce Snoopie, an instrumentation-based multi-GPU communication profiling tool built on NVBit, capable of tracking peer-to-peer transfers and GPU-centric communication library calls. To increase programmer productivity, Snoopie can attribute data movement to the source code line and the data objects involved. It comes with multiple visualization modes at varying granularities, from a coarse view of the data movement in the system as a whole to specific instructions and addresses. Our case studies demonstrate Snoopie's effectiveness in monitoring data movement, locating performance bugs in applications, and understanding concrete data transfers abstracted beneath communication libraries. The tool is publicly available at https://github.com/ParCoreLab/snoopie.

title: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field
summary: We introduce CABOT, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an active computing medium. In the classical Look-Compute-Move (LCM) model every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid once per robot. CABOT strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the grid holds a state from a finite set Q, the states evolve synchronously under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the Look operation returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 1, without multiplicity detection and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |Q|, rather than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required. On an inert floor (|Q| = 1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected, configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row, fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and indicate the range of the model.

title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.

title: Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting
summary: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let $n$ be the network size, $k$ the number of participants, and $d$ their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with $C$ colors yields completion within $(C-1)d+1$ slots and at most $nk$ transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound $Δ_0$ suffice for a $15(Δ_0+1)$-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic $Θ(d)$ completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives $O(d\min\{n,(Δ_0+1)^2\log n\})$ slots when $n$ is known. Independent random transmission gives $O((Δ_0+1)(d+\log(k/η)))$ slots with failure probability at most $η$; for fixed $Δ_0$, this simplifies to $O(d+\log(1/η))$. A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most $b$, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most $2b-1$, with matching examples.

title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads
summary:
Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance.
  A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
comment: To appear in 2027 IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA)
summary:
Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$μ$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering.
  We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).

title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
summary:
Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it.
  We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.
